title: Closed Tram Stop
aka: Remove Nth Node From End of List
story: A tram line's route is stored as a chain of stops, from the first stop to the terminus. Each stop only knows the next stop on the line.

Roadworks close a stop, and the notice from the city counts from the far end: "the 3rd stop before the end of the line, counting the terminus as 1st". The route system must skip that stop. It reads the route once, from the front, because the route can be long and is shared with other systems.
task: Write closeStop(head, k). Remove the k-th node counting from the end of the list (k = 1 is the last node) and return the head of the updated list.
If the removed stop was the first one, the head changes. If it was the only stop, return an empty list (null / None). Try to do it in a single pass.
constraints: Stop ids are integers and may repeat.

examples.explanation: Counting from the end, 52 is 1st and 47 is 2nd. Remove 47, so 35 now points straight to 52.
The 3rd stop from the end of a 3-stop line is the first stop. There is no stop before it to relink, so the new head is 24.

hints: To remove a node from a singly linked list, which node do you actually need to be standing on?
You need the node just before the closed stop, so you can set its next to skip one. If you knew the length n, that node is n - k steps in. Can you find it without knowing n?
Imagine two walkers on the route with exactly k stops between them. When the front walker steps off the end, where is the back walker?

Put a dummy node before the head (it handles removing the first stop). Move lead forward k steps from the dummy, then move lead and trail together until lead.next is null. Now trail.next is the closed stop: set trail.next = trail.next.next and return dummy.next.
bruteForce: Walk the whole route once to count the stops, n. The closed stop is number n - k + 1 counting from the front, so walk again to the stop just before it and relink that one.

That is O(n) and correct, so the problem is not speed in big-O terms. It reads the route twice, though, and the city's system only wants one read. The gap trick does the same job in one pass, and the same idea finds "the k-th last item" of any stream you can read only once.

js: * function ListNode(val, next) { this.val = val; this.next = next; }
* ListNode is already defined for you.
* @param {number} k  position counted from the end (1 = last)
py: # ListNode is already defined for you.
def close_stop(head: ListNode, k: int) -> ListNode | None:

tests.note: the only stop closes: the line is empty
first stop of two: the head itself is removed
k equals the length: remove the head
identical stop ids: remove by position, not by value

js: const dummy = new ListNode(0, head); // lets us remove the first stop too
for (let i = 0; i < k; i++) lead = lead.next; // open a gap of k
trail.next = trail.next.next; // skip the closed stop
py: dummy = ListNode(0, head)  # lets us remove the first stop too
for _ in range(k):  # open a gap of k
trail.next = trail.next.next  # skip the closed stop
walkthrough: Keep two pointers a fixed distance apart. When the front one reaches the last stop, the back one is exactly k stops behind it, which is the stop just before the one to remove.
Trace 11 → 24 → 35 → 47 → 52 with k = 2. Start both pointers on a dummy node D placed before 11.
• Move both: lead = 52, trail = 35. Now lead.next is null, so stop.

Why the dummy: when k equals the length, the stop to remove is the head, and the node "before" it does not exist. With a dummy, trail stays on D and D.next = D.next.next removes the head like any other node. Forgetting this case is the most common bug here.
solution.timeWhy: lead walks the list once; trail follows behind it.
solution.spaceWhy: A dummy node and two pointers.
solution.takeaway: To find a position measured from the end of a linked list in one pass, keep two pointers a fixed gap apart. And to delete a node, stand on the node before it, using a dummy head so the first node is not a special case.
